intro: Twelve verses written from a desert and remembering a sanctuary. The superscription puts David in the wilderness of Judah, and the psalm takes its images from exactly there: thirst, dry ground, night, and animals that feed on the dead. For a learner it drills one thing, the second person suffix -kha attached to a verb: I seek You, I have beheld You, I will bless You, I remember You, my lips praise You. Five different verbs, one ending. Watch also the word nefesh, soul or throat, which appears four times and changes state each time: it thirsts, it is satisfied, it clings, and at the end it is the thing the enemies are hunting.

stichs.en: A psalm of David.
When he was in the wilderness of Judah.

verses.summary: The superscription places the prayer in a named desert, which turns the thirst of the next verse into a physical fact and a figure at once.

stichs.en: O God, You are my God; I search for You at first light.
My soul thirsts for You, my flesh longs for You,
in a parched and weary land with no water.

verses.summary: Three claims stacked in one breath: God addressed, soul, flesh. The land supplies the vocabulary, and the verb of seeking carries the word for dawn inside its root.

stichs.en: So I have looked for You in the sanctuary,
to see Your strength and Your glory.

verses.summary: A memory of the sanctuary, recalled from its exact opposite. What was seen there is named as strength and glory, and it is what he is looking for now.

stichs.en: For Your steadfast love is better than life;
my lips shall praise You.

verses.summary: The claim that gives the psalm its weight: a thing worth more than being alive. Everything after this verse is what a person does with such a claim.

stichs.en: So I will bless You as long as I live;
in Your name I will lift my palms.

verses.summary: Blessing offered during a lifetime, since life has just been ranked second. Lifted palms are the standard posture of prayer, named here rather than described.

stichs.en: My soul is filled as with fat and rich food,
and my mouth praises with lips of glad song.

verses.summary: Satisfaction described in the vocabulary of the altar and the feast, by a man in a place with no water. The hunger is answered in words, not food.

stichs.en: When I remember You on my bed,
I murmur over You through the night watches.

glosses: in the watches of the night
verses.summary: The scene shifts to night and to a bed. The prayer leaves the remembered sanctuary for the one place where nobody is watching.

stichs.en: For You have been my help,
and in the shadow of Your wings I sing for joy.

verses.summary: The reason given is help already received, not rescue expected. The wings are a bird's over the nest before they are anything else.

stichs.en: My soul clings close behind You;
Your right hand holds me up.

verses.summary: Two clauses describing one grip from both ends: the soul holding on from below, the right hand holding up from above.

stichs.en: But those who seek my life, to ruin it,
shall go down into the depths of the earth.

verses.summary: The enemies appear only now, in the last three verses, and they are described going down in the same breath in which the speaker is held up.

stichs.en: They shall be handed over to the power of the sword;
they shall be a portion for foxes.

verses.summary: The fate is left in the passive, with no named agent and no gloating. What the verse describes is a battlefield after everyone has gone.

stichs.en: But the king shall rejoice in God;
all who swear by Him shall glory,
for the mouth of liars shall be stopped.

verses.summary: The psalm closes by stepping out of the first person to speak of the king in the third. The last thing granted to the enemy is silence.

pardes.body: The psalm is one continuous address, and it travels through the body. It begins in the throat with thirst, {{2.4}}, moves out to the flesh, then to the lips and the mouth in verses 4 to 6, then to a bed at night in verse 7, then to a hand holding the speaker upright in verse 9. Only in verse 10 does anyone else enter, and the enemies are shown going down into the earth in the same movement in which the speaker is held. The final verse steps out of the first person for the king, and it is the psalm's only sentence about the public world.

{{2.3}} is the crux. Its root can be read as the ordinary verb for seeking, and it is also the root of the noun for dawn, so translators split between I seek You earnestly and I seek You at daybreak. Both are defensible from the consonants, and both suit a psalm that will name the night watches later. {{6.1}} is the fat of an animal, the portion burned on the altar, so the satisfaction of verse 6 is described with the vocabulary of an offering by a man with neither altar nor water. Verse 11 gathers the difficulties: {{11.0}} is rare enough that translations disagree over whether the sense is poured out, handed over or hurled, and {{11.5}} is the ordinary word for foxes, though most modern readings take it here as jackals, which are the scavengers a battlefield actually attracts.

The plural in {{7.4}}, the night watches, drew a discussion of its own: the Talmud at Berakhot 3a preserves a dispute over whether the night divides into three watches or four. The superscription sends the reader back to the books of Samuel, but it does not say which flight is meant, and commentators split between David hiding from Saul and David leaving Jerusalem during Absalom's revolt. Either way verse 12 is read as the sentence of a man who holds a crown and has no throne, and the sanctuary of verse 3 as a memory rather than a building he can walk into, which makes the whole psalm a model for prayer said in the wrong place.

{{4.2}}, better than life, is the line the mystical reading turns on. If that love is worth more than existence, then existence is not the highest term, and the thirst of verse 2 stops being a lack to be fixed and becomes the accurate perception of a soul that has ranked its wants correctly. The dry land of {{2.11}} is then a condition rather than a geography, the state in which nothing at all is available except the wanting. {{9.0}}, clinging, is the verb Genesis uses for a man joined to his wife and Deuteronomy for holding fast to God, and the two halves of verse 9 describe that single bond from both directions: the soul reaching up from below, the right hand holding from above.
